Celtic languages. An ancient Indo-European language family spoken across the British Isles, Brittany, and the Iberian Peninsula. Once dominant across much of Europe, they were displaced by Latin and Germanic languages. Today, a handful of survivors including Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh, and Breton persist largely through cultural revival and legislative protection. Celtic languages encode the identity and heritage of Celtic peoples and remain at the center of cultural nationalism in Ireland and Scotland.

Celtic languages split into two main branches: Insular, which includes Irish, Scottish Gaelic, and now-extinct Pictish, and Brythonic, which includes Welsh, Breton, and now-extinct Cornish. Irish, called Gaeilge, is an official language of the Republic of Ireland with roughly five hundred thousand speakers. It is compulsory in schools but often spoken as a second language. Welsh is the most robust Celtic language with roughly nine hundred thousand speakers, about thirty percent of Wales' population. Welsh-medium education and media have sustained it more effectively than other Celtic languages.

Scottish Gaelic, called Gàidhlig, has roughly fifty-seven thousand speakers, concentrated in the Outer Hebrides. It was suppressed after the seventeen forty-six Jacobite defeat but has seen modest revival. Breton, called Brezhoneg, is spoken by roughly two hundred thousand people in Brittany, France. It is a distinct branch and has no official status in France, complicating preservation efforts.

Linguistically, Celtic languages are SVO, subject-verb-object, and undergo initial consonant mutation called lenition, features distinctive within Indo-European. Language revival movements in Ireland, Scotland, and Wales have restored limited functionality to Celtic languages through education, media, and cultural activism, though they remain endangered.
